module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierce%E2%80%93Birkhoff_conjecture)

The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture asserts that any piecewise-polynomial function can be expressed
as a maximum of finite minima of finite collections of polynomials. It was first stated in 1956
by Garrett Birkhoff and Richard S. Pierce, though the modern rigorous formulation is due to
Melvin Henriksen and John R. Isbell.

The conjecture has been proved for `n = 1` and `n = 2` by Louis Mahé.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace PierceBirkhoff

/--
A set is semi-algebraic in `ℝⁿ` if it can be described by a finite union of sets, each defined by
finitely many simultaneous multivariate polynomial equations and strict inequalities.
-/
def IsSemiAlgebraic {n : ℕ} (S : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι : Type) (p₀ p₁ : ι → Finset (MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ)), Finite ι ∧
    S = ⋃ i, {x | (∀ p ∈ p₀ i, MvPolynomial.eval x p = 0) ∧
      ∀ p ∈ p₁ i, MvPolynomial.eval x p > 0}

/--
A set is semi-algebraic in `ℝ` if it can be described by a finite boolean combination
of polynomial equations and inequalities.
-/
def IsSemiAlgebraic₁ (S : Set ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι₀ ι₁ : Type) (p₀ : ι₀ → Polynomial ℝ) (p₁ : ι₁ → Polynomial ℝ), Finite ι₀ ∧ Finite ι₁ ∧
    S = (⋃ i, {x | Polynomial.eval x (p₀ i) = 0}) ∪ ⋃ i, {x | Polynomial.eval x (p₁ i) > 0}

open scoped Polynomial

/--
A function `f : ℝⁿ → ℝ` is piecewise polynomial if there exists a finite covering of `ℝⁿ` by
closed semi-algebraic sets such that the restriction of `f` to each set in the covering is
polynomial.
-/
def IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι : Type) (P : ι → Set (Fin n → ℝ))
    (g : ι → MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ),
    Finite ι ∧
    (∀ i, IsClosed (P i)) ∧
    (∀ i, IsSemiAlgebraic (P i)) ∧
    (⋃ i, P i) = Set.univ ∧
    ∀ᵉ (i : ι) (x ∈ P i), f x = MvPolynomial.eval x (g i)

/--
A function `f : ℝ → ℝ` is piecewise polynomial if there exists a finite covering of `ℝ` by
closed semi-algebraic sets such that the restriction of `f` to each set in the covering is
polynomial.
-/
def IsPiecewisePolynomial (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (ι : Type) (P : ι → Set ℝ)
    (g : ι → Polynomial ℝ),
    Finite ι ∧
    (∀ (i : ι), IsClosed (P i)) ∧
    (∀ (i : ι), IsSemiAlgebraic₁ (P i)) ∧
    (⋃ (i : ι), P i) = Set.univ ∧
    ∀ᵉ (i : ι) (x ∈ P i), f x = Polynomial.eval x (g i)

/--
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture states that for every real piecewise-polynomial function
`f : ℝⁿ → ℝ`, there exists a finite set of polynomials `gᵢⱼ ∈ ℝ[x₁, ..., xₙ]` such that
`f = supᵢ infⱼ(gᵢⱼ)`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 13]
theorem pierce_birkhoff_conjecture {n : ℕ} (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ)
    (hf : IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f) :
    ∃ (ι κ : Type) (g : ι → κ → MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ), Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧
      ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, MvPolynomial.eval x (g i j) := by
  sorry

/--
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 1`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 13]
theorem pierce_birkhoff_conjecture_dim_one (f : ℝ → ℝ)
    (hf : IsPiecewisePolynomial f) :
    ∃ (ι κ : Type) (g : ι → κ → Polynomial ℝ), Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧
      ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, Polynomial.eval x (g i j) := by
  sorry

/--
The Pierce-Birkhoff conjecture holds for `n = 2`.
This was proved by Louis Mahé.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 13]
theorem pierce_birkhoff_conjecture_dim_two
    (f : (Fin 2 → ℝ) → ℝ) (hf : IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f) :
    ∃ (ι κ : Type) (g : ι → κ → MvPolynomial (Fin 2) ℝ), Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧
      ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, MvPolynomial.eval x (g i j) := by
  sorry

end PierceBirkhoff

status_issues.recorded: @[category research open]. The statement asserts the conjecture for every n.
status_issues.source_status: Claimed disproved in September 2026, in a preprint with a Lean 4 formalization: Z. Lai, L.-H. Lim, J. Ren, "Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture is false", arXiv:2609.10420 (v1, 9 Sep 2026). The counterexample lives on Sym²(ℝ⁵) × Sym²(ℝ⁵) ≅ ℝ³⁰. Put P = XY, q_{ij,±} = P_ii ± 4P_ij, and h = min of the 40 forms. Then f = h where h > 0 and det X > 0, and f = 0 elsewhere. This f is continuous and piecewise quadratic, and has no finite max–min representation by polynomials of any degree. The authors also give constructions for n = 5, 6, 7, 8, 72. The cited source, Wikipedia, has not recorded this: its last edit was 16 Feb 2026, and it still describes the conjecture as proved only for n = 1, 2.
status_issues.evidence: arXiv abstract and TeX source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10420. I read the 30-dimensional proof and found no gap: the separation lemma via radial limits, the quadratic orbit lemma, and the two perturbations X_±Y_± = ε²I with det X_± of opposite signs. Formalization: https://github.com/7pocheR/Pierce-Birkhoff (n=30_d=5_k=2/lean). Its theorem `pierce_birkhoff_counterexample30` states `∃ f : (Fin 30 → ℝ) → ℝ, Continuous f ∧ Nonempty (FiniteClosedPolynomialCover f) ∧ ¬ IsPolynomialLattice f`. Its 39 source files (6,234 lines) contain no sorry, admit, axiom or native_decide. In /workspace/review/bridge.lean I copied its definitions verbatim and proved, without sorry, that this statement implies ¬(∀ f : (Fin 30 → ℝ) → ℝ, IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f → ∃ ι κ g, Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, eval x (g i j)). I also checked that `Bridge.bridge h (fun f hf => PierceBirkhoff.pierce_birkhoff_conjecture f hf) : False` typechecks. So their theorem contradicts this file's statement at n = 30, and adding dummy variables extends the counterexample to every n ≥ 30. Caveats: I could not build their project locally (it pins Lean v4.34.0-rc1 and a different Mathlib; the local toolchain is v4.33.1). The preprint is two weeks old and not peer-reviewed. The authors describe the 30-dimensional proof as human-checked and the 5–7-dimensional ones as under ongoing review.
status_issues.suggested_change: After maintainers vet the disproof, retag as `@[category research solved, AMS 13, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/7pocheR/Pierce-Birkhoff"]`. Replace the statement with its negation, e.g. `¬ ∀ (n : ℕ) (f : (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ), IsPiecewiseMvPolynomial f → ∃ (ι κ : Type) (g : ι → κ → MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ), Finite ι ∧ Finite κ ∧ ∀ x, f x = ⨆ i, ⨅ j, MvPolynomial.eval x (g i j)`. Optionally add `research open` variants for the dimensions not settled (n = 3 and 4; also up to 29 if the unreviewed low-dimensional examples are not yet trusted). Cite arXiv:2609.10420 in the docstring. `pierce_birkhoff_conjecture_dim_one` and `_dim_two` are unaffected.

reformulations.difference: The source asks for "a finite set of polynomials g_ij with f = sup_i inf_j g_ij". The Lean (here and in `_dim_one` and `_dim_two`) instead uses a rectangular family `g : ι → κ → MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℝ`: one inner index type κ is shared by every i, `ι κ : Type` are required to be `Finite`, and the sup/inf are Mathlib's conditionally complete `⨆`/`⨅` on ℝ. On an empty index type those return `sSup ∅ = sInf ∅ = 0`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For nonempty finite ι and κ the range is finite, hence bounded, so `⨆`/`⨅` are the true max/min. Ragged rows J_i, each nonempty as the source's inf requires, can be padded to a common κ by repeating an entry of the row, since min is idempotent. Any finite index set reindexes into `Fin k : Type`. If ι or κ is empty, the right-hand side is identically 0. So the junk case only represents f ≡ 0, which also has the honest representation ι = κ = Unit, g = 0. The junk values therefore neither add nor remove representable functions. I checked the direction that matters in Lean: any Lean witness, junk cases included, yields a genuine finite max/min expression tree of polynomials (`Bridge.supinf_isPolynomialLattice` in /workspace/review/bridge.lean, no sorry). The padding direction is routine and not formalized.

reformulations.difference: Semi-algebraic sets are usually defined as the Boolean algebra generated by polynomial sign conditions. The Lean definition uses a normal form instead: a finite union of basic sets {x | p(x) = 0 for p ∈ A, q(x) > 0 for q ∈ C}.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This is the standard normal form (Bochnak–Coste–Roy, Prop. 2.1.8). I proved it in Lean: `Bridge.isSemiAlgebraic_iff : PierceBirkhoff.IsSemiAlgebraic S ↔ Bridge.IsSemialgebraic S`. Here `Bridge.IsSemialgebraic` is the inductive closure of the sets {p ≤ 0} under complement, binary union and binary intersection, copied verbatim from the Lai–Lim–Ren Lean development. The proof is in /workspace/review/bridge.lean and uses only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

reformulations.difference: The docstring says "finite boolean combination of polynomial equations and inequalities". The definition, however, only allows a finite union of zero sets {p = 0} and positivity sets {p > 0} of univariate polynomials, with no intersections or complements. It is used in `IsPiecewisePolynomial` and `pierce_birkhoff_conjecture_dim_one`, which state the n = 1 case on ℝ with `Polynomial ℝ` rather than on `Fin 1 → ℝ` with `MvPolynomial (Fin 1) ℝ`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The semi-algebraic subsets of ℝ are exactly the finite unions of points and open intervals, possibly unbounded. Each piece is a zero set or a positivity set: {a} = {X − a = 0}, (a,b) = {(X − a)(b − X) > 0}, (a,∞) = {X − a > 0}, (−∞,b) = {b − X > 0}, ℝ = {1 > 0}. Conversely, every zero set and positivity set is semi-algebraic. So `IsSemiAlgebraic₁` is exactly the class of semi-algebraic subsets of ℝ; for example [a,b] = {(X−a)(b−X) = 0} ∪ {(X−a)(b−X) > 0}. Transporting along ℝ ≅ (Fin 1 → ℝ) and ℝ[X] ≅ MvPolynomial (Fin 1) ℝ, `pierce_birkhoff_conjecture_dim_one` is exactly the n = 1 case. Semi-algebraicity of the pieces is redundant anyway. Given any finite closed cover with f polynomial on each piece, f is continuous. f then equals one polynomial on each connected component of the complement of the zero sets of the pairwise differences. The closures of those components form a closed semi-algebraic cover. I checked the definitions in Lean on f = |x| = max(x, −x) (/workspace/review/scratch1.lean), but did not prove the general equivalence.

review.notes:
I found no misformalization. The four definitions match Lucas–Madden–Schaub–Spivakovsky's definition (arXiv math/0601671), which is the primary reference cited by Wikipedia: a finite cover of ℝⁿ by closed semi-algebraic sets with a polynomial on each piece. Continuity follows automatically, as that paper notes. The three theorems state the Henriksen–Isbell formulation that Wikipedia quotes. The two dimension variants are exactly the n = 1 and n = 2 cases.

Lean checks (in /workspace/review):
- scratch1.lean: |x| satisfies `IsPiecewisePolynomial` and equals a Lean `⨆ ⨅` of polynomials. Empty `⨆`/`⨅` on ℝ give 0. The n = 0 case of the main theorem is trivial. The definitions are satisfiable and non-degenerate.
- bridge.lean: `isSemiAlgebraic_iff` (the file's definition matches the standard Boolean-algebra one) and `bridge` (the Lai–Lim–Ren formal statement implies the negation of the main theorem at n = 30). Neither uses sorry.

The only substantive item is the status issue above. It is a very recent claimed disproof with a Lean formalization; the cited Wikipedia page does not record it yet. I could not build the external Lean project because its toolchain differs from the local one.

Minor, not reported as a finding: the `dim_one` docstring credits n = 1 to Mahé, as Wikipedia does. zbMATH's review of Mahé 2007 calls n = 1 "practically trivial"; that is attribution only, and the `research solved` tag is right.
